brief.topic: The Odd Loop That Makes Two Colors Impossible

s01: Can we color every dot with one of two colors, so every connection joins different colors?
Start with this square.
Make one corner teal.
Its neighbor must be coral.
The next is teal, and the last is coral.
The final connection works.
Four steps bring us back with the right color.
Now try a triangle.
Teal, coral, teal.
The last connection joins two teal dots.
Changing the first color only exchanges the names of the colors; it does not remove the conflict.
Each edge switches the required color.
An even loop switches an even number of times and returns consistently.
An odd loop asks the starting dot to be the opposite of itself.
This obstruction is also the whole story.
In a graph with no odd cycle, choose a starting dot in each connected piece.
Color dots by whether their distance from that start is even or odd.
An edge joining equal parities would create an odd closed walk, which contains an odd cycle.
So two colors work exactly when the graph has no odd cycle.
This is called a bipartite graph.
A single new diagonal turns our square into two triangles, and destroys the possibility.

scenes.narration:
Can we color every dot with one of two colors, so every connection joins different colors?

Start with this square. Make one corner teal. Its neighbor must be coral. The next is teal, and the last is coral. The final connection works. Four steps bring us back with the right color.

Now try a triangle. Teal, coral, teal. The last connection joins two teal dots. Changing the first color only exchanges the names of the colors; it does not remove the conflict.

Each edge switches the required color. An even loop switches an even number of times and returns consistently. An odd loop asks the starting dot to be the opposite of itself.

This obstruction is also the whole story. In a graph with no odd cycle, choose a starting dot in each connected piece. Color dots by whether their distance from that start is even or odd. An edge joining equal parities would create an odd closed walk, which contains an odd cycle.

So two colors work exactly when the graph has no odd cycle. This is called a bipartite graph. A single new diagonal turns our square into two triangles, and destroys the possibility.
